newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-World sugar market to remain in surplus - QSC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-World sugar market to remain in surplus - QSC.

text.p: The world sugar market was expected to remain in surplus in the short to medium term and to put pressure on sugar prices, Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC) said.

But consumption in the Asian region continued to grow faster than the world average and much of Queensland's production was likely to be sold to markets in this region, QSC said in its annual report for the year ended June 30.
QSC was confident of successfully marketing all 1996 season raw sugar, forecast to reach a record five million tonnes several years ahead of previous forecasts, it said.
The annual report shows raw sugar output in Queensland, which produces 95 percent of Australia's sugar, fell to 4.60 million tonnes from the 1994/95 record of 4.68 million tonnes.
This was despite record cane production and occurred after an 8.3 percent fall in average commercial sugar content, chief executive David Rutledge and chairman Robert Sutton said.
QSC's sugar sales revenue for the year slipped to A$1.99 billion from A$2.05 billion while total operating revenue fell to A$2.01 billion from A$2.07 billion.
At present it appeared that 1996 season pool prices would be about eight to ten percent lower than in 1995 because of the persistent global surplus, QSC said.
QSC's exports in the year to June 30 1996 slipped by 4.6 percent to 3.79 million tonnes, or 81 percent of raw sugar sales, from the record level of the previous year.
Major export destinations in 1995/96 were customers in Asia, which took 63.8 percent of exports, and North America/Canada, on 21.9 percent.
Traditional customers maintained their key position as major markets for Queensland raw sugar in the latest year, QSC said.
Canada overtook Japan to become QSC's largest export market in the latest year, taking 674,774 tonnes against 627,568 tonnes in 1994/95, statistics presented in the report show.
Japan, the second largest export market in 1995/96, took 662,910 tonnes against 679,610 tonnes in 1994/95, when it was QSC's largest export customer.
In 1995/96 Malaysia was QSC's third-largest export market, taking 583,017 tonnes, up from 538,034 tonnes the year before.
Then followed South Korea on 576,200 tonnes, down from 673,300 tonnes.
China sales fell sharply to 355,000 tonnes from 638,500 tonnes.
QSC was the major supplier of raw sugar to Canada, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore and Taiwan, it said.
Market share in Japan was about 40 percent while in other markets QSC supplied 50 percent or more of raw sugar imports.
In New Zealand and Taiwan it supplied 100 percent of imports, it said.

Long-term agreements of between three and five years were negotiated with some customers in 1995/96 but tonnages sold under guaranteed price arrangements continued to decrease because of the gradual breakdown of regulated domestic sugar regimes in most customer countries, it said.
QSC also further extended its customer base in 1995/96 with first sales made to six new customers, Croatia, Kazakstan, Latvia/Lithuania, Mexico and the Philippines.
New refineries were expected to start operations over the next 12 months or so in Saudi Arabia, Indonesia and Taiwan.
These could be expected to increase the raw sugar trade at the expense of white sugar and QSC hoped to supply raw sugar to the new refineries in 1996/97, it said.
Deregulation of sugar purchasing in some countries such as Morocco may provide new marketing opportunities, it said.
QSC sold 927,606 tonnes of raw sugar to domestic consumers in Australia in 1995/96, up 17.9 percent on the year before.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
